questions.stem: A prompt template wraps pasted material in tags, but each author uses different tag names for the same sort of text, and the instructions refer to them loosely. Which rule from the page fits?

options.text: Give each kind of input one meaningful label, used identically everywhere
options.says: One meaningfully named tag per kind of content, used the same way every time (module 6, page 2).

options.text: Vary the names, keeping any two sections from being mistaken for each other
options.says: Ruled out because "The names have no magic; they have to be meaningful and used the same way every time".

options.text: Drop the tags and rely on the order of the sections to mark the data
options.says: Ruled out because "Order is not a boundary".

options.text: Use numbered tags such as part1 and part2
options.says: Ruled out because the rule is "One tag per kind of content".

questions.stem: A prompt places a 30-page policy in the middle, with the instruction to list exceptions buried in a paragraph above it. The replies often summarise instead. Which edit helps most?

options.text: Add several paragraphs of background to make the exceptions stand out more
options.says: Ruled out because the page says "More context is not automatically better".

options.text: Write the instruction in capital letters but keep it inside the same paragraph
options.says: Ruled out because the page says "A key instruction buried in a long paragraph is easy to underweight".

options.text: Move the policy below the instruction, to be read most recently
options.says: Ruled out because the page advises "Place your long documents and inputs near the top of your prompt, above your query, instructions, and examples".

options.text: Give the task its own line, and restate it after the long material
options.says: A key instruction goes on its own line and is restated after long material (module 6, page 1).

origin.section: More context is not automatically better

questions.stem: A marketing lead gets a social post in the wrong tone, regenerates the same request four times, and keeps getting similar misses. What is the better method?

options.text: Regenerate the post more often and keep whichever result looks best
options.says: Ruled out because "Regenerating the same request and hoping is the reflex; revising the request is the method".

options.text: Rewrite the whole request from scratch each time, changing several parts together
options.says: Ruled out because the method is to "change one thing in the description", not several at once.

options.text: Switch to a larger model before touching the brief
options.says: Ruled out because the page advises "ask why before asking again".

options.text: Name the flaw, change one element of the brief and compare results
options.says: Revising the request one change at a time is the method, and re-rolling is the reflex (module 5, page 2).

questions.stem: A planner asks Claude to schedule five deliveries under several constraints and gets a wrong plan with no explanation. The planner wants to see where it went wrong, and a program reads only the final plan. Which prompt fits?

options.text: Ask the same question five times and keep the version with most agreement
options.says: Ruled out because "Comparing detects the variation; it does not remove it".

options.text: Ask for the result only, with no working shown at all
options.says: Ruled out because the page notes that "when an answer looks wrong, the steps tell you where it went wrong".

options.text: Ask for working first, then the result after a marker for code to take
options.says: Reasoning is requested before the answer and kept apart, so a program uses the answer while a person reads the steps (module 6, page 2).

options.text: Ask for working and result mixed in one paragraph
options.says: Ruled out because the page says to "Keep the reasoning separate from the answer".

questions.stem: A classifier prompt lists four allowed labels, but when a ticket fits none the model invents a fifth one. Which two changes address it? (Select two.)

options.text: Lower the temperature setting to make the answers vary less
options.says: Ruled out because "The models this course uses do not accept them".

options.text: Spell out the closed set in the output format
options.says: Say what to do when unsure, for example use unknown, and list the values as in "label is one of billing, bug, account, other" (module 6, page 2).

options.text: Ask the model to be more careful and precise in its choice
options.says: Ruled out because the page names "Stacking adjectives instead of constraints" as a trap.

options.text: Name a fallback value for when it is unsure
options.says: Say what to do when unsure, for example use unknown, and list the values as in "label is one of billing, bug, account, other" (module 6, page 2).

options.text: Remove the list and let the model pick the closest option freely
options.says: Ruled out because the page says to "use unknown" when unsure, "rather than leaving the model to invent a value".

options.text: The material, the question, the criteria and proof for each finding
options.says: Analysis wants the material, the question and the criteria, and the evidence for each conclusion (module 6, page 3).

options.text: Audience, tone, length and an example of the target style
options.says: Ruled out because the drafting task wants "Audience, tone, length, an example of the target style".

options.text: Named references, claims tied to them and gaps declared in the text
options.says: Ruled out because the research task wants "Sources named, claims tied to sources".

questions.stem: A prompt writer keeps mixing the rule "Use only the policy. One word." into the description of the response layout, and results wander. In the course's specification, where do rules that must hold belong?

options.says: Ruled out because the task part answers "What exactly is to be done now?".

options.text: In the role line, written at the start of the prompt
options.says: Ruled out because the role part answers "Who is doing the work?".

options.text: In the documents section, next to the material those rules cover
options.says: Ruled out because the documents part answers "What material to use?".

options.text: In a constraints part of its own, apart from the one that sets shape
options.says: Constraints answer "What must hold?" and the output format fixes the shape, so each is its own part of the specification (module 6, page 3).

questions.stem: A prompt says only "Make the tone better", and the reply is a more formal rewrite although the writer wanted it casual, and a rerun gives something different each time. Which cause does the course name, and what is its fix?

options.text: Ambiguity, so state the exact request and add constraints, an example and a format
options.says: A reasonable answer to a different question, with results that change from run to run, is ambiguity, and the fix is to "Say exactly what is wanted; add constraints, an example, a format" (module 6, page 4).

options.text: Missing context, so supply the facts, the readers and the purpose of the text
options.says: Ruled out because missing context shows as "Generic or invented content", not as a reasonable answer to the wrong question.

options.text: The wrong feature, so use a tool, retrieval or code in place of a longer prompt
options.says: Ruled out because the wrong feature is the case where "The job needs something the prompt cannot give".

options.text: The wrong model, so evaluate another tier or raise the effort setting for the work
options.says: Ruled out because the wrong model is "Correct instructions, correct context, still a capability or speed miss".

questions.stem: A charity's draft appeal describes the families it serves in a pitying tone. Which check from the non-profit list applies?

options.text: Whether the figures cited match the programme's own records
options.says: Ruled out because that check is "every claim about impact, every statistic and every funder requirement against the source".

options.says: Ruled out because "Donor and beneficiary records are sensitive".

questions.stem: A project manager asks Cowork for a one-page status pack and wants the reviewer to spot weak points quickly. Which line in the outcome description supports that?

options.text: Ask it to write with extra confidence, making the pack read as decisive
options.says: Ruled out because "Confidence of tone is not a signal".

questions.stem: A student notices that after a few exchanges with Claude, the thesis has shifted toward the conclusion that Claude kept suggesting. Which check from the student's list was missed?

options.text: Whether the rules of the course allow the amount of help that was used

options.text: Whether the tool is pushing a view rather than helping the author reach one

questions.stem: A clerk sends Claude a rotated, low-resolution photo of a handwritten delivery note and enters the quantities it reports without a second look. Which concern applies?

options.text: Models read handwriting reliably, so no concern arises

options.text: Such images invite mistakes or invention, so the entries need verifying
options.says: Low-quality or rotated images invite mistakes and invention, so the readings are verified (module 4, page 1).

options.text: The entries are safe if Claude is asked to say how sure it is of each one
options.says: Ruled out because "Self-reported confidence is not a measure of accuracy".

options.text: The entries are safe when the quantities are small whole numbers
options.says: Ruled out because "Do not use Claude for tasks requiring perfect precision or sensitive image analysis without human oversight".

questions.stem: Reviewers of a research assistant's answers want each claim to be traceable and any weak claim removed before reading. Which prompt addition fits?

options.text: A second run of each question to compare the two answers
options.says: Ruled out because "Comparing detects the variation; it does not remove it".

options.text: A score out of ten that the assistant gives to each answer it writes

questions.stem: A strategist uses Research mode for a vendor comparison and receives a report with a citation after each claim. Which step is still needed before it goes to the board?

options.says: Ruled out because Research needs "web search must be turned on".

options.text: None; every claim already has its citation
options.says: Ruled out because "a citation shows where an answer came from, not that the source is right".

options.text: Check the statements that would hurt if wrong against the sources cited
options.says: A citation shows where an answer came from, not that the source is right, so the statements that matter are checked against it (module 7, page 2).

options.text: Repeat the research several times and keep the statements that every run shares
options.says: Ruled out because "Comparing detects the variation; it does not remove it".

questions.stem: A team adds quotes, citations, an "I don't know" option and a restricted source list, and then tells users the answers no longer need review. Which two statements describe how the course treats that claim? (Select two.)

options.text: It is sound, because each technique adds an independent check in code
options.says: Ruled out because "The documentation's own techniques turn some of this into a prompt", not into a check in code.

options.text: It overreaches, since errors are reduced and not removed

options.text: It is reasonable if users are told to ask Claude how sure it is
options.says: Ruled out because "confidence is not evidence".

options.text: It is sound, because grounded prompts leave hallucinations at zero
options.says: Ruled out because the documentation says they "don't eliminate them entirely".

options.text: Checking stays, since these steps make it faster and do not replace it
options.says: The techniques are mitigations, and "These make checking faster; they do not replace it" (module 5, page 2).

questions.stem: An HR assistant uploads a group photo from a company event and asks Claude to name each person pictured for a directory. What should the team expect?

options.text: Names looked up from the staff files after Claude checks each face against them
options.says: Ruled out because what training gives excludes "Access to your files, systems or today's date".

options.text: Accurate names for everyone whose face is clear, with a note of uncertainty
options.says: Ruled out because "Claude cannot be used to name people in images, and refuses to".

options.text: Approximate names, with each face marked by pixel coordinates
options.says: Ruled out because "Coordinates and localisation outputs are approximate", and the refusal still applies.

questions.stem: Claude works through a multi-step pricing calculation and gives a confident chain of steps ending in a total. A single wrong step early on would spoil everything after it. What should decide whether the total is trusted?

options.text: The model's own statement that it re-checked each step it took
options.says: Ruled out because "Self-reported confidence is not a measure of accuracy".

options.text: A check outside that reasoning, such as a test or a second reader

options.text: A higher thinking setting for the same calculation

options.text: The length and detail of the steps shown to the reader

questions.stem: A retailer asks Claude to return pixel coordinates of price tags in shelf photos and crops each photo automatically. Some crops miss the tags by a few pixels. Which limit explains it?

options.text: Claude cannot read images under 200 pixels, so every tag is missed

options.text: Spatial answers are approximate, so each cut-out needs a margin or a check

questions.stem: A benefits chatbot answers from the company handbook, but some replies add rules borrowed from how other employers work. Which prompt instruction targets this?

options.text: Run each question three times and keep the answer that repeats most often
options.says: Ruled out because "Comparing detects the variation; it does not remove it".

options.text: Give it the role of an HR director with many years of experience
options.says: Ruled out because "A role is a request, not a credential".

options.text: Ask it to state how sure it is about each rule that it gives

questions.stem: A student uses Claude to find sources for an essay and pastes three citations into the bibliography, one of which does not exist. Which two habits would have prevented it? (Select two.)

options.text: Confirm each reference in a library or database
options.says: A student checks every fact and citation that goes into graded work, because a hallucination includes "an invented citation, a function that does not exist" (module 9, page 1).

options.text: Ask Claude whether each reference is real before using it
options.says: Ruled out because "Self-reported confidence is not a measure of accuracy".

questions.stem: A freelance writer uses Claude to draft a short story opening and wants to be sure it is safe to publish under their own name. Which check does the course name for creative work?

options.says: A step-by-step task on trusted live pages suits Claude in Chrome with manual approval and a clean profile (module 8, page 3).

options.text: Claude in Chrome with Skip all approvals switched on for speed
options.says: Ruled out because in that setting "Claude does not pause and nothing checks its actions".

options.text: Cowork on the whole drive with Auto approval, letting no single step wait
options.says: Ruled out because "A dedicated folder limits what an injected instruction or a mistake can reach".

options.text: Research mode with web search left open on all sites
options.says: Ruled out because Research suits "A job one document answers", and not a step-by-step task that the buyer wants to watch.

questions.stem: Six months ago a manager used plain chat for a one-off competitor summary. The work now repeats every week with the same rules and files. What does the course suggest?

options.text: Switch to Claude in Chrome to have the web pages reread each week
options.says: Ruled out because Chrome is for "A step-by-step task on a website you trust".

options.text: Keep using plain chat for the weekly job as before
options.says: Ruled out because the page says to "revisit it when the work changes".

options.text: Revisit the choice of tool, moving the routine into a Project or skill
options.says: A task that began as a one-off and became weekly deserves a Project or a skill (module 8, page 3).

options.text: Move to Cowork and let it run the weekly job on its own
options.says: Ruled out because "Picking the most powerful surface" is named as a trap.

questions.stem: A lecturer asks Claude to draft a marking rubric and then to grade the pupils' essays against it, and records the grades. What stays with the lecturer under the course's guidance?

options.text: Little: Claude can mark and record the essays
options.says: Ruled out because the educator "Owns: what students are taught, how they are assessed and the fairness of grades".

options.text: The final signature, once Claude has produced each mark for the class
options.says: Ruled out because "Judging student work and decisions with consequences for a student stay with the educator".

options.text: The first draft of the rubric, with the grading handed over
options.says: Ruled out because the usage policy treats "academic testing and admissions as a high-risk use needing human review".

options.text: Evaluating the work and any decision that affects the learners
options.says: Judging student work and consequential decisions stays with the educator (module 9, page 1).

questions.stem: A team lead tags Claude in a thread to compile a report, then closes Slack for the evening. A colleague adds a correction as a later message. Which two statements describe what happens? (Select two.)

options.text: Replies posted afterwards are followed
options.says: Tasks run in the cloud, "Claude keeps working after you close Slack", and once in a thread it follows every reply (module 8, page 2).

options.text: It ignores the late addition, reading only the tagged post
options.says: Ruled out because it reads "the thread it was tagged in (including earlier messages when mentioned mid-thread)" and not only the tagged post.

options.text: Work stops once Slack is closed on the lead's device
options.says: Ruled out because tasks "run in the cloud on Anthropic's servers; sessions can continue when your computer is offline".

options.text: It needs a fresh tag before it reads anything new
options.says: Ruled out because a thread it has joined needs no new tag, because "once it is in a thread it follows every reply".

options.text: The work carries on in the cloud
options.says: Tasks run in the cloud, "Claude keeps working after you close Slack", and once in a thread it follows every reply (module 8, page 2).

questions.stem: A new team member wants Claude to produce the entire quarterly customer review, from data pull to final slides, in one go on day one. What does the delegation guidance suggest?

options.text: Hand over the entire job in one go on day one
options.says: Ruled out because "A good draft does not show the figures were right".

options.text: Hand over a small, clear step whose result shows, then widen it
options.says: Decide how much to hand over at once: a small, clear step with a visible result is easier to judge, so start narrow and widen (module 5, page 1).

options.text: Hand over only the final slides, with the data pulled
options.says: Ruled out because the figures need "Exact numbers, authoritative source" from code or an analyst.

options.text: Hand over everything but ask for a confidence note at the end
options.says: Ruled out because "Self-reported confidence is not a measure of accuracy".

questions.stem: An operations lead wants to package the team's meeting-notes format so that Claude applies it whenever relevant, and has no programmer available. What is needed?

options.text: A script in Python that calls the API once for each set of notes
options.says: Ruled out because "A simple custom skill needs no code".

options.text: Markdown instructions in the required folder structure, zipped and uploaded
options.says: A simple custom skill needs no code: Markdown instructions in the required folder structure, zipped and uploaded (module 7, page 2).

options.text: A connector to the notes folder with write access for the assistant
options.says: Ruled out because skills are "folders of instructions, scripts and resources that Claude loads dynamically".

options.text: A plugin built by a partner company for note-taking and shared with the team
options.says: Ruled out because partner skills are "From other companies, built to work with their connectors".

questions.stem: A team builds a Project knowledge base from a forwarded summary, a draft policy and a thick scan with unreadable pages. Which principle did they ignore?

options.text: Judge the material first, preferring approved primary text
options.says: Quality in is quality out: prefer final approved text, primary documents and short clean files (module 7, page 1).

options.text: Remove superseded versions from the knowledge base
options.says: Ruled out because "Two versions of one document side by side invite Claude to quote either", and the stem lists no duplicates.

options.text: Name an owner and a review date for each file
options.says: Ruled out because "nothing alerts you when a file goes stale", which is about upkeep and not about the quality of what goes in.

options.text: Cite the source in each answer given to a reader of the Project
options.says: Ruled out because "a citation shows where an answer came from, not that the source is right".

questions.stem: A team wants Claude to use a connector that reads a local application on one employee's machine, not a service on the internet. Which shape fits?

options.text: A skill that bundles the application's instructions for Claude to load
options.says: Ruled out because skills are "folders of instructions, scripts and resources that Claude loads dynamically".

options.text: A custom connector in the directory, which Anthropic has already verified
options.says: Ruled out because "a custom connector has not been verified by Anthropic".

options.text: A desktop extension, which hosts its endpoint on that same computer
options.says: Desktop extensions are for the desktop app only and run a server locally, while remote connectors reach a server from Anthropic's cloud (module 7, page 3).

options.text: A remote connector, which reaches an MCP server from Anthropic's cloud
options.says: Ruled out because remote connectors "reach an MCP server from Anthropic's cloud, not from your device".

questions.stem: A power user has connected twelve connectors and notices conversations feel crowded with tool lists. Which two statements fit the help centre's suggestion? (Select two.)

options.text: Blocked removes every tool from the list for good
options.says: Ruled out because the page describes how "connector tools are loaded", and blocked is a permission instead.

options.text: Needs approval loads each tool only after the user has clicked
options.says: Ruled out because needs approval is a permission, and "require a human click before it writes to it" says nothing about when tools load.

options.text: Always allowed keeps the lists short by hiding the prompts
options.says: Ruled out because "each tool can be always allowed, needs approval or blocked" is a permission rule, not a loading mode.

options.text: Load each integration only when the work needs it
options.says: The page suggests On demand "when you have ten or more connectors" (module 7, page 3).

options.text: Ten or more is the point where it pays off
options.says: The page suggests On demand "when you have ten or more connectors" (module 7, page 3).

questions.stem: A team's Project holds a pricing file that nobody has reviewed for a year, and answers drift out of date without any alert. Which practice would have prevented it?

options.text: Telling Claude in the instructions to flag old files whenever it notices them
options.says: Ruled out because "nothing alerts you when a file goes stale".

options.text: Naming an accountable person for each source and fixing a recurring check
options.says: Each source needs an owner and a review date, because nothing alerts you when a file goes stale (module 7, page 1).

options.text: Uploading the file again whenever somebody happens to remember to do it
options.says: Ruled out because a stale file should be "a missed appointment, not a surprise".

options.text: Keeping every earlier version in the Project in case it is needed
options.says: Ruled out because "Old and new documents side by side give Claude two sources to quote".

questions.stem: An analyst sets a formatting convention in the Excel add-in's instructions, then finds the Word add-in ignores it. Why?

options.text: Excel instructions work only when macros are enabled in the workbook
options.says: Ruled out because "Macros and VBA, and data tables, are unsupported".

options.text: Cross-app work is switched off, which blocks every instruction from passing between apps
options.says: Ruled out because cross-app work concerns files, through "Let Claude work across files".

options.text: Each one keeps its own rules, so the setting does not carry into another app
options.says: Instructions are set per add-in and do not carry from Excel into Word or PowerPoint (module 8, page 2).

options.text: Word needs an Enterprise plan before it can read any instructions
options.says: Ruled out because the add-ins are "installed from Microsoft AppSource, for the paid plans".

questions.stem: A paid-plan Project nears its context limit, yet it keeps answering from its large knowledge base. What does the help centre describe, and what follows from it?

options.text: It retrieves the relevant parts, so muddled files spoil replies at scale
options.says: Near the limit the paid plans switch on retrieval of the relevant parts, and a retrieved passage is only as good as its source (module 7, page 1).

options.text: It drops the oldest files one by one until the whole Project fits again
options.says: Ruled out because Claude "enables RAG mode, retrieval of the relevant parts" and does not remove files.

options.text: It folds every file into the instructions and deletes the original files
options.says: Ruled out because retrieval "expands the Project's capacity" and leaves the originals in place.

options.text: It stops accepting questions until enough files have been removed
options.says: Ruled out because "A big knowledge base is possible" under that mode.

questions.stem: A freelancer on a Pro plan asks whether Anthropic uses their chats to improve Claude. What does the course say?

options.text: Only for incognito chats, which feed improvements to the models
options.says: Ruled out because "Incognito chats are not used to improve Claude".

options.text: Only if they opt in, or a conversation is flagged
options.says: Consumer chats are used only if the user allows it in privacy settings, or if a conversation is flagged (module 10, page 1).

options.text: Never, whatever settings they have chosen or plan they hold
options.says: Ruled out because "By default Anthropic does not use inputs or outputs from commercial products to train models" applies to Team, Enterprise and the API.

options.text: Always, with no setting available to stop the use in any plan
options.says: Ruled out because chats are used "only if you choose to allow it in your privacy settings".

questions.stem: A user sets Claude in Chrome to its least restrictive approval mode to save clicks while browsing a bank site. Which two statements does the page support? (Select two.)

options.text: Claude still reviews each action for safety and blocks anything unsafe
options.says: Ruled out because that is the automatic mode, where "Claude keeps working and reviews each action for safety".

options.text: It is advised for sites visited often, such as a bank
options.says: Ruled out because the habit is to "prefer Manually approve for anything that matters".

options.text: It suits only complete trust
options.says: Skip all approvals means nothing checks the actions, so it is for complete trust only, and the habit is "do not manage financial accounts, legal documents or medical information through it" (module 8, page 2).

options.text: Nothing checks what is done
options.says: Skip all approvals means nothing checks the actions, so it is for complete trust only, and the habit is "do not manage financial accounts, legal documents or medical information through it" (module 8, page 2).

options.text: Downloads and sensitive entries are still skipped silently there
options.says: Ruled out because even then "certain things still need your explicit approval".

questions.stem: A manager wants to paste an unreleased financial forecast, marked confidential, into a chat tool that the company has sanctioned. Which rule fits?

options.text: Ask Claude to forget the forecast afterwards, which satisfies the rule
options.says: Ruled out because "An instruction to forget is not a control".

options.text: Treat it as internal, so any tool that is approved is fine for everyone
options.says: Ruled out because confidential examples are "Contracts, unreleased financials, customer lists".

options.text: Treat it as regulated, with no tool ever allowed to receive it
options.says: Ruled out because the regulated class holds "Health records, payment-card data, government IDs, personal data under GDPR".

options.text: Permitted there for those who need it, often with identifiers removed
options.says: Confidential data goes only in approved tools, with a need to know and often with identifiers removed (module 10, page 1).

questions.stem: A security lead wants Claude in chat and Cowork to stop reaching the open web for everyone, without disabling the apps. Which control do the pages describe?

options.text: A lookup-feature switch that account owners set organisation-wide
options.says: Owners can turn web search off for chat and Cowork (module 10, page 2).

options.text: A sites allowlist in the browser extension, which also covers chat and Cowork
options.says: Ruled out because "Claude in Chrome sites can be allow-listed or blocklisted".

options.text: A retention setting that deletes browsing history after thirty days
options.says: Ruled out because the table lists "Retention settings, including custom retention or zero data retention for Enterprise agreements".

options.text: A per-user prompt telling Claude not to use the internet
options.says: Ruled out because "A prompt is a request, not a guarantee".

questions.stem: An assistant asks a user to confirm "Send this email to everyone on the list?" while the user works through a long task and presses Allow without a glance. Which two statements does the course support? (Select two.)

options.text: It matters only if the email carries an attachment or a link
options.says: Ruled out because the page says to "Use Manual approval for sending, deleting, buying and posting", whatever the email carries.

options.text: It is a formality that was settled when the task began
options.says: Ruled out because "Do not press Allow out of habit".

options.text: It is harmless: classifiers already screen every action
options.says: Ruled out because "the risk is not zero".

options.text: Approving unread hands approval to whatever was injected
options.says: The confirmation prompt is the control, and the habit is to "read each confirmation before agreeing" (module 10, page 2).

options.text: The prompt is the control
options.says: The confirmation prompt is the control, and the habit is to "read each confirmation before agreeing" (module 10, page 2).

questions.stem: A team lead tags Claude in a public channel and asks it to summarise what the finance team said in their private channel. What will happen?

options.text: It reads the private room through the tools that an admin connected
options.says: Ruled out because "Where you tag decides what it can use and who sees the result".

options.text: It searches the private room as a person would
options.says: Ruled out because "Private channels and DMs are read only from inside them".

options.text: It summarises from a Slack canvas shared in the public room
options.says: Ruled out because "A Slack canvas is not readable".

options.text: It cannot search that conversation
options.says: Claude Tag reads other public channels only by searching, and private channels and DMs only from inside them (module 8, page 2).

questions.stem: A campaign group plans to have Claude send thousands of personal-looking messages to voters that hide their automated origin. Which prohibited category on the policy's list fits?

options.text: Compromising privacy or identity of private persons
options.says: Ruled out because that category covers "sharing personal information without consent".

options.text: Criminal-justice, censorship and surveillance uses
options.says: Ruled out because that category covers "tracking a person's location without consent or scoring people's trustworthiness".

options.text: Undermining democratic processes, such as deceptive content
options.says: The policy lists undermining democratic processes, such as deceptive political content or automated messages that hide their artificial origin (module 10, page 1).

options.text: Fraudulent, abusive or predatory practices aimed at customers
options.says: Ruled out because that category lists "phishing, fake reviews, falsified documents".

questions.stem: A consultant sends a client a market summary drafted with Claude, and the client's own policy asks suppliers to say when AI helped. The consultant says nothing. Which responsibility was skipped?

options.text: Data care, such as keeping client files out of the chat
options.says: Ruled out because "Do not put in what you may not share; anonymise first".

options.text: Accountability for the accuracy of what is sent to the client
options.says: Ruled out because "An error in AI-assisted work is your error to correct".

options.text: Fairness and impact on the people the summary covers
options.says: Ruled out because the duty is to "Consider who is affected by the work".

options.text: Being honest about the tool's part when a rule demands it
options.says: Disclosure: be honest about the AI's part when it matters to them, when a policy requires it or when they ask (module 5, page 2).

questions.stem: A company builds an autonomous agent that acts on customers' behalf, and its lawyer asks whether the Usage Policy's rules apply when no person reads each output. What does the page say?

options.text: Only the high-risk requirements apply
options.says: Ruled out because the policy has "universal usage standards that apply to everyone".

options.text: Unattended operation must still conform, and extra guidance exists for it
options.says: The policy has universal standards, high-risk requirements and additional guidelines for chatbots, minors, agentic use and MCP servers, and agentic use must still comply (module 10, page 1).

options.text: The policy covers chatbots and nothing else, so an agent falls outside its reach
options.says: Ruled out because it adds guidelines for "chatbots, products serving minors, agentic use and servers built on the Model Context Protocol (MCP)".

options.text: The rules apply only when a person reads each output before it is used
options.says: Ruled out because "agentic use must still comply with the policy".

questions.stem: A researcher uses Research mode all morning and then finds the usage limits nearly exhausted, though ordinary chats were few. What explains it?

options.text: Research runs on the free plan, which gives a smaller allowance than paid chat
options.says: Ruled out because Research "needs a paid plan (Pro, Max, Team or Enterprise)".

options.text: Memory was switched on, which re-reads every earlier chat each time it answers
options.says: Ruled out because memory "holds preferences and context that Claude picked up" and does not re-read old chats.

options.text: Research is billed separately, so the ordinary limits are left untouched by it
options.says: Ruled out because "Research counts against the same limits as ordinary chat".

options.text: It retrieves many sources, which drains allowances faster than simple talk
options.says: Research counts against the same limits as ordinary chat but can use them up faster because it retrieves many sources (module 7, page 2).

origin.section: Research: many linked searches, with citations

questions.stem: A multi-turn assistant on Claude Opus 5.5 with thinking active fills its window sooner than the team expected, though visible replies are short. What contributes?

options.text: Earlier thinking is stripped each turn, so only the latest turn matters
options.says: Ruled out because current Opus, Sonnet and Fable models "keep them by default".

options.text: Earlier reasoning is retained by default and takes up room
options.says: Thinking tokens count toward the context window, and current Opus, Sonnet and Fable models keep earlier thinking by default (module 4, page 2).

options.text: Visible replies are billed twice, so they fill the space twice over
options.says: Ruled out because "each user message and assistant response accumulates in the window", once and not twice.

options.text: Thinking is stored on the server, so it never reaches the request at all
options.says: Ruled out because "It lives in the context".

questions.stem: On a Team plan, an analyst's Excel conversation cannot write into the open Word memo, though the add-in works fine in each app. What is the likeliest cause?

options.text: The cross-file setting is off by default there, and set per device
options.says: "Let Claude work across files" is off by default for Team and Enterprise, on by default for Pro and Max, and set per device (module 8, page 2).

options.text: Excel instructions carry into Word, so the two sets must have conflicted
options.says: Ruled out because a formatting convention "does not carry into Word or PowerPoint".

options.text: Claude can open and switch files itself, so the memo must have been locked
options.says: Ruled out because it "cannot open, create or switch files itself".

options.text: Word memos can be read by Claude only through a cloud platform
options.says: Ruled out because "Cross-app work is not supported through Bedrock, Vertex AI, Azure AI Foundry or an LLM gateway".

questions.stem: A nightly job that summarised last month's reports now fails with a "prompt is too long" error on this month's larger reports, using the same code. Which statement fits?

options.text: Raising the output limit enlarges the window, so the job will then pass
options.says: Ruled out because "Raising it does not enlarge the window".

options.text: The request is accepted anyway and simply ends with a stop reason
options.says: Ruled out because "the API returns a 400 invalid_request_error" when the input alone exceeds the window.

options.text: The input alone exceeds the window, so it must shrink or the window grow
options.says: Input that alone exceeds the window is refused with a 400 error on every model (module 1, page 1).

options.text: A newer tokenizer shrank the text, so the same words now fit more easily
options.says: Ruled out because "the same text produces about 30 percent more tokens than on earlier models".

questions.stem: A request with thinking active returns an answer cut off mid-sentence, though the output limit was set generously and the input is small. Which two statements explain it? (Select two.)

options.text: The input exceeded the window, which ends the request with an error
options.says: Ruled out because "max_tokens is a cap on output, not on context".

options.text: Reasoning tokens count against the same cap
options.says: Thinking tokens are "billed as output tokens" and leave less room for the visible answer inside max_tokens (module 1, page 1).

options.text: The model reached a word count that Claude sets for answers
options.says: Ruled out because the loop ends when "the output reaches the max_tokens limit you set", a limit the caller chooses.

options.text: Less room is left for the visible text
options.says: Thinking tokens are "billed as output tokens" and leave less room for the visible answer inside max_tokens (module 1, page 1).

options.text: Thinking text is free, so it leaves the budget alone
options.says: Ruled out because the output Claude generates for the turn, "including its extended thinking, counts too".

questions.stem: A summarisation job on Claude Opus 5.5 sends short inputs but generates long answers, and the bill is higher than planned. Which price fact points to the lever?

options.text: Output tokens are free once the window is not full, so length is harmless
options.says: Ruled out because the tokens are "billed as output tokens".

options.text: Input and output tokens share one price, so only the prompt length matters
options.says: Ruled out because the lineup lists "Price per million tokens, input / output".

options.text: Each produced token costs about five times a fed-in one, so brevity pays most
options.says: The table lists Claude Opus 5.5 at $4 input and $20 output per million tokens, so output costs five times as much and shorter answers save the most (module 3, page 1).

options.text: A larger window cuts the price of each output token, so a bigger model saves money
options.says: Ruled out because "Larger windows raise the ceiling; they do not remove the need to decide what goes in".
